name: Xiuhuitzolli
material: Wood frame covered in turquoise mosaic
powers: Sign of divine kingship; only the tlatoani may wear it.
description: The xiuhuitzolli is the pointed diadem of turquoise mosaic worn by the Aztec tlatoque, the supreme rulers, as the emblem of sovereignty, its name meaning 'pointed thing of turquoise.' The right to wear it was held to come from the gods and to pass with the kingship, and colonial accounts record that the ruler Motecuhzoma was crowned with one at his accession. The Codex Mendoza and the Florentine Codex show the crown above a headband of the same mosaic, and the turquoise itself was a material charged with solar and divine significance, gathered through long-distance trade and set by master lapidaries. The xiuhuitzolli was one element of a full regalia that included the nose-piece, ear-plugs, and the royal cloak, and its loss at the conquest was read as the end of legitimate Aztec rule. Surviving turquoise mosaic crowns and their fragments are among the most treasured objects of the museums of Mexico and Europe, and the diadem remains the icon of Aztec sovereignty.

name: Xalam Lute
material: Wood, skin, gut or nylon strings
description: The xalam is a plucked five-string lute of the Wolof of Senegal, with a calabash or carved wooden bowl body, a skin head, and strings grouped into two melody and three rhythm strings. Played by griots (gewel), it produces the interlocking lines that back praise-songs, genealogies, and narrative epics, and its twanging rhythms support both festive dance music and the serious recitation of lineage history. Across the Sahel the same instrument appears under other names, such as the hoddu of the Fulani and the khalam, with each people tuning and playing it in its own idiom. A griot's xalam was far more than entertainment: the words carried by the strings could flatter, mock, or counsel, making the instrument the audible badge of the praise-singer's craft. Older songs survive within griot families, while contemporary musicians have carried the xalam onto popular stages, keeping the sound of praise orature alive in Senegal and the diaspora.

name: Xhosa Beadwork
description: Xhosa beadwork of South Africa is made with imported glass beads sewn onto leather, cotton, or cloth supports to create necklaces, aprons, headdresses, and panels of dress worn at the great passages of life. At initiation, the beads speak: the colours and patterns worn by a young man in the circumcision school, and by the women who celebrate his return, carry coded messages of love, status, and clan that are meant to be read by the initiated. Married women wear beadwork that records their lineage and their husband's house, while older styles of white and blue bands gave way to the bright colour families of the modern era. Beadwork was a woman's art, taught by mothers and grandmothers, and its patterns changed with fashion while keeping their social grammar. Today Xhosa beadwork is worn at weddings, initiation feasts, and church festivals, and the beaded garments of the Red Xhosa communities of the Eastern Cape remain the most photographed tradition. Cooperatives and designers now sell Xhosa beadwork across South Africa and abroad.
